items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Danish naming is patronymic before ~1850: 'Mikkel Nielsen' means Mikkel son of Niels, so the father's given name is Niels — the patronymic alone does not identify which Niels.
Vital events are recorded in parish church books (kirkeboeger); baptism entries name both parents. Civil registration is much later.
The Stagstrup parish register is only ~3% name-indexed on FamilySearch — plan to browse the register images by year rather than rely on the index.

entry.jurisdiction: Stagstrup Sogn, Hassing Herred, Thisted Amt, Denmark
entry.rationale: Mikkel's baptism was recorded on 20 Aug 1779 in Stagstrup Sogn. Danish parish registers (kirkebøger) name both father and mother in the baptism entry — making this the most direct and highest-probability source for the father's full name and identity. The Stagstrup register (image group 004130616, 1763–1814) is only ~3% name-indexed on FamilySearch (loc_001 quirk): the name index cannot be relied upon, so the register images must be browsed to August 1779. The patronymic 'Nielsen' confirms the father's given name was Niels; this record will establish his full name, including any farm or toponym surname. Watch for variant spellings of 'Blyeberg' (e.g., Blieberg, Bliiberg, Blyebjerg).

Per loc_001: Danish lægdsruller enroll every male from early childhood under the father's name, with each son's entry directly beneath the father's — making the rolls direct parentage evidence for a male subject. Mikkel (b. 1779) would appear in the earliest surviving rolls from 1789 (age ~10) under his father Niels's household entry. Image group 004748896 covers Thisted Amt lægd districts 1789–1814 and is 0% name-indexed — images must be browsed. The roll will name the father Niels and likely give his farm or surname, completing the identification begun by the patronymic. Also accessible via Rigsarkivet arkivalieronline (sa.dk) if FamilySearch images are unclear.

The 1787 Denmark census was taken when Mikkel was ~8 years old and almost certainly residing in his father's household. The census records all household members with age and relationship to head, providing indirect co-residence evidence of parentage. FamilySearch collection 1401625 is fully indexed and free — a quick, high-value check. Search for head-of-household 'Niels' in Stagstrup Sogn (or adjacent Hassing Herred parishes if Stagstrup returns no result). Transcriptions also available at the free Dansk Demografisk Database (ddd.dda.dk) as a cross-check.

The 1801 Denmark census was taken when Mikkel was ~22. If he had not yet set up his own household he may still appear in his father Niels's household; even if living separately, locating his household will show neighbours and farm context that cross-reference the father. The 1801 census explicitly records each person's relationship to the household head. FamilySearch collection 1401625 is fully indexed and free. Compare any result against the 1787 household found in item 3.

FAN item — the creator is Mikkel's father Niels; the deliverable is Mikkel identified as a named heir, which is direct parentage evidence. Stagstrup Sogn lies in Hassing Herred; probate records (skifteprotokoller) for this herred are held in image group 004392710 (Hassing Herred, 1690–1850, browse-only). A skifteprotokol opened on father Niels at his death would enumerate all children as heirs. The date window is set by the father's plausible lifespan: a man whose son was born in 1779 could have died anywhere from shortly after 1779 to c. 1839 (age ~80+). FamilySearch collection 2015318 holds the probate indexes — search for a 'Niels' in Hassing Herred within this window, then browse the corresponding images.

Fallback for item 1. The Thisted Amt parish registers (including Stagstrup) are freely browsable at Rigsarkivet arkivalieronline (sa.dk) independently of FamilySearch. If the FamilySearch image for August 1779 is missing, damaged, or illegible, the Rigsarkivet copy of the same register may be clearer or carry additional folios. Browse the Stagstrup kirkebog for August 1779 baptisms and look for Mikkel's entry naming his father.
